title: ELI’S SONS WERE PRIESTS—And Were Accused of Sleeping With Women at the Tabernacle Entrance
paragraphs: ELI’S SONS WERE PRIESTS—And Were Accused of Sleeping With Women at the Tabernacle Entrance

They wore the garments. They handled the sacrifices. They stood near holy things. But Scripture says they did not know the LORD. And somewhere inside this ancient scandal is a warning for every person who has ever looked religious while secretly drifting from God.
There are Bible stories we soften because the unfiltered version makes us uncomfortable.
This is not one of those stories.
The sanctuary was supposed to be safe.
People came to Shiloh carrying sacrifices, prayers, gratitude, guilt, grief, hope.
They came looking toward God.
And standing near the sacred place were priests.
Men who knew the ceremonies.
Men who understood the rituals.
Men who belonged to a respected religious family.
Men whose father was Eli, the priest.
Their names were Hophni and Phinehas.
And then Scripture says something devastating about them:
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:12, KJV
Read that again slowly.
They were priests.
But they did not know the LORD.
They knew the sanctuary.
They knew the sacrifices.
They knew priestly privilege.
They knew religious language.
They knew how worship worked.
But they did not know God.
And perhaps that is the first wound this story opens in us.
Because it is possible to become familiar with the things of God without surrendering to God Himself.
You can know worship songs and not worship.
You can quote verses and resist the One those verses reveal.
You can attend church while protecting a secret life.
You can post Scripture publicly while starving spiritually privately.
You can say “God bless you” while bitterness is eating you alive.
You can know Christian vocabulary, Christian culture, Christian people, Christian routines...
and still desperately need Christ.
That is why this story is not merely about two corrupt priests who lived thousands of years ago.
It is about the terrifying distance that can exist between appearing close to God and actually knowing Him.
And what happened at Shiloh became darker.

Hophni and Phinehas were abusing their priestly position surrounding the sacrifices. First Samuel 2:13–17 describes servants taking meat from worshipers and even demanding portions before the fat prescribed for sacrifice had been offered. When a worshiper objected, the response could become a threat: surrender the meat now, or it would be taken “by force.”
Scripture does not describe their behavior as a minor procedural mistake.
It says:
“Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:17, KJV
Very great.
Before the LORD.
These men were taking something sacred and turning it into something that served their appetites.
And that pattern should frighten every Christian leader, every ministry, every preacher, every content creator—and every believer.
Because spiritual corruption often begins when we quietly reverse the direction of worship.
Instead of asking,
“How can I serve God?”
we begin asking,
“How can the things of God serve me?”
Recognition.
Money.
Influence.
Sex.
Power.
Attention.
Control.
Admiration.
A platform.
A reputation.
The appetite changes, but the temptation is ancient.
Holy things become tools for feeding unholy desires.
Then we arrive at one of the most disturbing sentences in the chapter.
The traditional Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 2:22 reads:
וְאֵת אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכְּבוּן אֶת־הַנָּשִׁים הַצֹּבְאוֹת פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד
Transliterated in part:
ve’et asher-yishkevun et-hannashim hatzove’ot petach ohel mo’ed.
In straightforward English, the crucial words describe how they “lay with” the women who served or assembled at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.

The verb behind “lay,” שָׁכַב (shakhav), can mean to lie down and, in contexts such as this construction, is used as a euphemism for sexual relations. The traditional Hebrew text therefore gives us the basis for translations that say Eli’s sons “slept with” or “lay with” these women.
The King James Version renders the verse:
“Now Eli was very old, and heard all that his sons did unto all Israel; and how they lay with the women that assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.” — 1 Samuel 2:22
That accusation is in the medieval Masoretic Hebrew textual tradition underlying most Old Testament translations, and many modern English Bibles retain it.
But if we are going to defend Scripture rather than exploit Scripture, there is something else you deserve to know.
There is an ancient textual question here.

The Greek Septuagint form of this verse does not contain the latter clause accusing the sons of sleeping with the women. The NET Bible's textual note also observes that the clause appears to have been absent from the surviving evidence of the Dead Sea Scroll manuscript 4QSamᵃ, based on the available space in the manuscript.
That matters.
It does not mean we should erase the words preserved in the Masoretic tradition.
It means we should possess enough reverence for Scripture to tell readers where the manuscript evidence deserves careful handling.
The Hebrew Masoretic text explicitly contains the sexual accusation.
The surviving Septuagint tradition represented here does not.
So we should not pretend there is no textual question.
And yet the central indictment against Hophni and Phinehas does not depend upon that disputed clause.
That is crucial.
Long before verse 22, Scripture has already condemned them.
They are introduced as men who “knew not the LORD.”
Their corruption surrounding the sacrifices is described.
Their sin is called “very great.”
Their contempt for the LORD's offering is established.
Eli later confronts the evil reports concerning his sons, and the biblical narrative moves relentlessly toward judgment.
The scandal is bigger than sex.
The deeper scandal is that men representing God were living as though God did not matter.
And that is where this ancient story stops being comfortable.
Because perhaps you have never stolen meat from an altar.
Perhaps you have never worn an ephod.
Perhaps nobody has ever called you a priest.
But you know what it feels like to maintain an appearance while something underneath it is dying.
Maybe nobody knows what you watch when the door closes.
Nobody knows about the messages.
Nobody knows about the resentment.
Nobody knows about the addiction.
Nobody knows how cold your prayer life has become.
Nobody knows how long it has been since you opened Scripture because you actually wanted God rather than because you wanted something to post.
Nobody knows about the compromise you keep renaming so you do not have to call it sin.
And maybe the most frightening thing is this:
you have become good at looking okay.
Hophni and Phinehas teach us that proximity to sacred things is not the same as holiness.
A church building cannot save you.
A Christian family cannot save you.
A ministry position cannot save you.
A baptism certificate cannot save you.
Your theology books cannot save you.
Your Christian posts cannot save you.
Your pastor cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
And that is where this story becomes more than scandal.
Because if we stop with Eli’s sons, all we have is a warning.
But the Bible does not end at Shiloh.
The story keeps moving.
Human priests fail.
Human leaders fail.
Religious institutions fail.
Fathers fail.
Sons fail.
We fail.
And Scripture keeps carrying us forward until another Priest appears.
Jesus Christ.
Not a priest who uses worshipers to satisfy Himself.
A High Priest who gives Himself for sinners.
Not a priest stained by his own corruption.
A High Priest who is holy.
Not a mediator who needs someone to atone for His sins first.
The sinless Son of God who becomes the sacrifice.
Hebrews says of Christ:
“For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners...” — Hebrews 7:26, KJV.
Do you see the contrast?
At Shiloh, corrupt priests were taking.
At Calvary, Jesus was giving.
They used sacred privilege for themselves.
Jesus “made himself of no reputation” and humbled Himself unto death.
They treated sacrifice with contempt.
Jesus became the sacrifice.
And while nails tore through His hands and the weight of human sin fell upon Him, the cross announced something our shame desperately needs to hear:
Your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin is serious.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is not fragile.
Grace does not mean God looks at evil and shrugs.
Look at the cross.
The cross tells us sin is so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
But the cross also tells us sinners are so deeply loved that Christ willingly came to rescue those who could never rescue themselves.
That is the Gospel.
Not “hide better.”
Not “look religious.”
Not “repair your image.”
Repent.
Come into the light.
Stop negotiating with the thing destroying you.
Stop decorating chains Jesus died to break.
Stop confusing church attendance with surrender.
Stop mistaking familiarity with Christianity for intimacy with Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe this article found you while you are hiding something.
Maybe your secret has never reached another human ear.
Maybe you have convinced everyone around you.
Maybe you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
One that people see.
And one that only God sees.
Listen carefully.
God already knows.
And you are still being called to come.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus came precisely because sin matters more than we could repair and grace reaches farther than we could climb.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV.
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
That does not turn repentance into cheap words.
Biblical repentance turns us toward God.
It stops defending what God calls sin.
It stops demanding darkness while asking God for peace.
It brings the wound into the light.
It trusts Christ.

And sometimes repentance also means seeking help, making restitution, establishing boundaries, confessing to those appropriately involved, stepping away from positions we have abused, or accepting consequences rather than using religious language to escape them.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying people.
Grace transforms.
And perhaps somebody reading this was not the person abusing religious power.
Maybe you were wounded by someone who did.
Maybe somebody carrying a Bible betrayed you.
Maybe someone behind a pulpit manipulated you.
Maybe somebody you trusted spiritually crossed boundaries that should never have been crossed.
Maybe your pain became tangled with your picture of God.
Please hear the distinction Scripture itself forces us to make:
Hophni and Phinehas were priests.
But their corruption did not reveal God's character.
It violated it.
Do not mistake a corrupt representative for the Christ they failed to represent.
Jesus is not Hophni.
Jesus is not Phinehas.
Jesus is not the leader who wounded you.
Jesus is not the hypocrite who disappointed you.
Jesus is not the Christian who betrayed your trust.
Look at Jesus Himself.
The One who welcomed the broken.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who touched the rejected.
The One who forgave sinners.
The One who laid down His life.
The One who walked out of the grave.
And maybe that is the most beautiful reversal in this entire story.
Scandal does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Sin does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
The thing you are ashamed to name does not possess authority to write the ending of your life.
Jesus does.
Be honest.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes one small act of honesty becomes the moment we stop pretending we do not need help.
And somebody reading the comments may discover they are not fighting alone.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God.
Your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
There are truths we understand differently when the night becomes dark.
Come back when shame starts whispering.
Come back when temptation starts bargaining.
Come back when you are tempted to believe you have gone too far.

If you want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, one practical way you can participate in Gospel work is by helping sound biblical truth travel farther—through prayer, faithful sharing, encouragement, and, if you freely choose, financial support.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Not because an algorithm deserves your obedience.
But because the Gospel is worth carrying beyond ourselves.
If one person encounters the truth of Christ because you refused to keep something life-giving to yourself, that share mattered.
You can still share.
You can still comment and encourage another struggling believer.
You can still point someone toward Jesus.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be an audience watching a few people do ministry.
We are the body of Christ.
And the world has already seen enough religious performance without transformed hearts.
It has seen enough titles without character.
Enough platforms without accountability.
Enough appearance without surrender.
Enough people standing near holy things while living far from a holy God.
The answer is not abandoning Jesus because religious people failed.
The answer is returning to Jesus because religious people fail.
Hophni and Phinehas stood near the sanctuary and did not know the LORD.
So perhaps the question haunting this chapter is not whether you attend church.
Not whether you own a Bible.
Not whether people think you are Christian.
Not whether you can explain theology.
The question is painfully simpler:
Do you know Him?
Not merely know about Him.
Know Him.
Have you surrendered?
Have you repented?
Are you trusting Christ rather than your religious appearance?
And if the answer exposes something uncomfortable tonight, do not run deeper into hiding.
Run to Jesus.
The same Bible that refuses to hide the scandal also refuses to end humanity's story with scandal.
There is a cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
The robes could hide the priests’ corruption from people for a while—but no robe can hide the heart from God, and no scandal surrendered to Christ is beyond the reach of redeeming grace.
